name: Bianca Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca, 43, and I lead the difficult electrical repairs in homes and shops. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the strongest practical workers here, on typical pay for the trade. My partner works at a plant nursery, our children are ten and fourteen, and we have a mortgage and four months of expenses saved. There are some other electrical employers nearby, and I use AI daily for checked notes and parts comparisons while keeping the safety decisions with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then the useful little tools can get on with being useful. I use AI daily to organise checked notes and compare parts descriptions. I'd still rather show an apprentice how to find a fault than give a lecture about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our normal wages cover the mortgage and bills, and we've got four months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for the trade, and my partner's nursery work is mostly potting and moving plants. I don't see this mild picture threatening either wage, and there are some other electrical firms nearby if I ever need to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the difficult home and shop repairs. Starting now I'd continue checking each AI-prepared note against my test readings before sending it. In the first year I'd keep the same work and household budget rather than buy equipment to make a quiet story feel exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with room to enjoy an ordinary week. I don't need every tool to become a new career before I'm allowed to like it. A correct repair and dinner at home are a decent result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you bring to the difficult calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the best practical electricians at the firm. I lead the work and know when the crew needs to stop and check again. That responsibility doesn't get handed to the machine because it can write a tidy note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the household behind dinner at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I have children aged ten and fourteen and a mortgage. The four-month reserve covers ordinary expenses, not a plan to stop earning forever. I like the children seeing a trade done properly without being told they must copy mine.

say: I'd keep **useful small tools** without demanding that each one becomes a new career.
I'd teach **fault-finding** beside the apprentice rather than turn every lunch break into a future lecture.
think: Our **regular wages** cover bills, with four months saved and some other local firms available.
My partner's **hands-on nursery work** also looks secure in this mild picture, so I don't expect a household wage shock.
do: Keep **leading difficult repairs** in homes and shops through the first year.
Continue checking daily **AI-prepared notes** against my test readings before sending them.
feel: **Calm** about present household work and money, with interest in useful tools and ordinary family life.
S0.quote: A correct repair and dinner at home are a decent result.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on covered bills, two continuing wages and a moderate reserve rather than higher pay or unlimited employment options.
She retains **high technical standing** and full credentials, while routine daily AI checks remain continuation rather than new learning.

steps.text: Keep leading difficult repairs and checking daily AI notes against actual readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's test whether a tool really saves us a second visit, not just whether it writes quickly. I'd offer to try the new approved AI fitting-identifier on returned parts, with every rating checked. A customer shouldn't have to pay for us ordering something that merely looks right in a photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage looks safe over the next few years because the physical repair diary is full. My partner's work is physical too, though I wouldn't promise either job is safe forever. I think there's room to benefit from useful tools without immediately losing our living, and I'd like a small financial stake in wider business growth too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a paid four-week fitting-tool trial now with normal weekly pay and hours unchanged, using returned parts before any live order. I'd also invest 40 monthly in a broad share fund that owns pieces of many businesses, only from spare earnings, after checking fees with my partner's agreement and leaving the four-month reserve untouched. In the first year I'd keep repairs and stop the tool trial if it missed required ratings, without treating fund returns as household wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our wages and interested in two small tests I can afford to stop. I wouldn't pick one fashionable company and call its shares the family's future. Owning a little of a fund isn't the same as knowing what next year's return will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does checking the fund mean before paying in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fees, what it holds and whether we can afford the whole monthly amount to fall in value. My partner and I would agree the budget, and the mortgage and ordinary bills come first. If we needed that 40 for essentials, I wouldn't invest it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the fitting tool gives a convincing wrong answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the trial and show the actual part and the required rating beside the suggestion. A photograph isn't permission to fit an unsafe part. The approved information and my own checks would still decide the order.

say: I'd judge the **fitting tool** by correct orders and avoided return visits rather than writing speed.
I'd protect **customers** from paying for a part chosen because a photograph looked convincing.
think: Our **near-term wages** look safe while both jobs remain physical and the repair diary is full.
I want a small **fund investment** without pretending a return or either job lasts forever.
do: Request a paid **four-week trial** of the approved AI tool on returned parts, retaining normal weekly pay and hours.
Invest **40 monthly** only from spare earnings with checked fees, partner agreement and the four-month reserve untouched.
Keep **paid repairs**, stop the trial for missed ratings and exclude uncertain fund returns from household wages.
feel: **Calm** about near-term wages, with curiosity and limits on both work and money experiments.
S1.quote: Owning a little of a fund isn't the same as knowing what next year's return will be.
fieldNote: Her **positive response** follows expected secure earnings, while the fund uses genuinely spare money and is not described as guaranteed income.
The **new AI trial** retains paid time, unchanged wage and hours, returned-part evidence and a stop rule for missed safety ratings.

steps.text: Request a paid four-week trial identifying returned fittings with the approved AI tool
Retain normal weekly pay and hours; stop trial if required ratings are missed
Invest 40 monthly from surplus only with checked fees, partner agreement and four-month reserve untouched
Keep paid repairs while excluding uncertain fund returns from household wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031, so being good with tools isn't a lifetime exemption. I'd tell the children we still value learning, without naming one safe occupation. I'd want the owner to explain actual paid work rather than sell us either fear or reassurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could fall once robots compete for the ordinary installation jobs that fill the diary. My partner's plant work could face the physical change too. Four months saved gives us time to respond, but I don't know the machine prices or how quickly either employer would buy one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep new fund payments off the plan for now, leaving that future money uncommitted rather than call a transfer new saving. I'd stop my 30 monthly leisure-clothes purchases and deposit that 30 only while actual earnings covered essentials. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep actual paid repairs and review both wages monthly before making a new financial commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the two wages, but not certain we lose everything. I'd rather hold a little room to choose than announce a rescue before I know what it costs. I can enjoy trying tools and still decide not to buy anything today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop replacing necessary work clothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, required protective equipment and worn-out work clothes stay in the ordinary budget. I'm talking about the extra shirt or jacket I buy for leisure, not safety. The deposit would stop if essential bills needed that money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would not buying fund units count as extra saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, changing where an existing planned payment might go doesn't create more household money. The only extra deposit I've named comes from spending less on leisure clothes. I want the numbers to mean what I say they mean.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from robots around 2031 without treating practical skill as a lifetime exemption.
I'd ask about **actual paid work** while keeping the children's choices open.
think: Both **physical wages** could shrink once capable robots compete for installations and plant work.
Our **four-month reserve** gives response time, while purchase prices and employer adoption remain unknown.
do: Make **no new fund commitment** now, without calling an unmade investment extra saving.
Stop **leisure-clothes purchases** and save 30 monthly only after actual wages cover essentials, preserving necessary work clothing.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and review both wages monthly before new commitments.
feel: **Anxious** about household earnings, with a plan that preserves choice without assuming certain total loss.
S2.quote: The only extra deposit I've named comes from spending less on leisure clothes.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **new saving** from investment reallocation, while protecting necessary work clothing and stopping the deposit if essentials need it.
Her **anxiety** follows plausible own and partner wage loss with retained control, not an asserted catastrophic loss or assumed robot adoption date.

steps.text: Wait on any new fund commitment until actual work and household costs are clearer
Save 30 monthly from leisure clothes only after essentials, keeping necessary work clothing funded
Keep actual paid repairs after 2028 and review both wages monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets me separate a long-term financial choice from a rushed answer to a work scare. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and robots around 2034. I'd keep learning useful tools, but I wouldn't borrow to make an investment look bigger or a qualification look urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own repair wage to remain steady over the next few years, with some other employers nearby and time to judge changes. I'd be 48 in 2031, with children about fifteen and nineteen, so the household would still need income. I'm uneasy about later robot competition, not expecting the fund to replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the 40 monthly fund payment only from genuine spare earnings, with checked fees, my partner's agreement and the four-month reserve untouched. I'd review actual pay and essential bills before each payment, pausing it if the budget needed the money. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid repairs and judge any new work tool from real jobs before paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the longer trade, but able to make a measured choice now. I like the idea of owning a small piece of many businesses rather than guessing which company wins. I also like knowing exactly which money we're not putting at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a five-year warning guarantee time to recover an investment loss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't know what markets would do or when we'd need money. Our four-month emergency reserve isn't money for the share fund. If the spare 40 didn't really feel spare, I wouldn't put it in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children have to copy your trade or your investment choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd explain what I know and what I don't. I'd want them to learn a useful skill and understand a bill, but their choices would be theirs. I won't promise my master electrician's licence predicts their working lives.

say: I'd distinguish a **long-term investment choice** from a rushed answer to a work scare.
I'd keep **borrowing out** of experiments rather than enlarge a risk to make a plan look impressive.
think: My **near-term repair wage** looks steady, with some local options and time to judge change.
At **48**, I'd still need household income and couldn't expect a small fund to replace wages.
do: Invest **40 monthly** only from genuine surplus with checked fees, partner agreement and the four-month reserve untouched.
Check **pay and essentials** before each payment, pausing investment if the household needs the money.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and judge tools from actual work before paying for them.
feel: **Uneasy** about later robot competition, with a measured financial choice that excludes emergency money.
S3.quote: Our four-month emergency reserve isn't money for the share fund.
fieldNote: The **fund choice** remains conditional on real surplus and continuing affordability, with no claim that a five-year warning guarantees market recovery.
She retains **wage dependence** and family autonomy, rather than treating high skill, a licence or a small investment as inherited career security.

steps.text: Invest 40 monthly from surplus only with checked fees, partner agreement and four-month reserve untouched
Keep paid repairs after 2031 and pause investing whenever essentials need the money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to learn and change without turning every family conversation into a race. I'd still want apprenticeships to teach a real skill and pay a wage people can live on. I'd let the children see different work rather than tell them my trade has a permanent claim on their future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when robots followed, so retirement isn't a checked solution. Our current wages cover the month and the four-month reserve gives room for ordinary problems. I feel secure over the next few years while admitting the later jobs and any fund value remain uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the same 40 monthly fund plan only with genuine surplus, checked fees, my partner's continuing agreement and the reserve untouched. We'd review the household budget each year as well as check essentials before every payment. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep actual paid repairs and pause investment whenever wages no longer left the money spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, with no need to act certain about the rest of my life. I can prepare and still spend a Sunday doing something the children chose. I don't want readiness to become a reason never to enjoy what the wage is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children being older make you less careful with the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't know what help they'll need or what the mortgage balance will be. We'd read the actual figures when the time came. I wouldn't replace the emergency account with a promise that grown children cost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if your partner stopped agreeing with the investment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pause the new payments and talk it through. My partner's agreement to a share fund isn't a box we tick once for ten years. I want a family plan both adults understand, not a fund balance one person has to defend.

say: I'd use **ten years** for real learning and family choices rather than turn preparation into a constant race.
I'd value **paid apprenticeships** without directing the children into my trade as a permanent guarantee.
think: Current **wages and reserves** make the next few years secure while later jobs and investment values remain uncertain.
I can't assume **retirement** at 53 or when robots follow around 56 resolves our mortgage or family costs.
do: Invest **40 monthly** only from surplus with checked fees, continuing partner consent and the four-month reserve untouched.
Review **household costs** yearly and check essentials before every payment, pausing if money or agreement is absent.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 without counting a fund return or adult children's earnings as replacement wages.
feel: **Calm** about near-term finances, with room to prepare and enjoy family life without claiming the later outcome is known.
S4.quote: My partner's agreement to a share fund isn't a box we tick once for ten years.
fieldNote: Her **near-term calm** rests on covered household costs, while future retirement, adult-child support needs and fund returns remain explicitly unpromised.
The **investment conditions** persist across the decade, including continuing consent and a pause if essentials use the surplus.

steps.text: Invest 40 monthly from surplus only with checked fees, continuing partner consent and four-month reserve untouched
Keep paid repairs after 2036 and pause investing if essentials or partner disagreement require it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could affect the physical work behind both our wages before we've had long to adjust. Honest paid-hour information and useful practical learning while earning would help. I'd want clear costs and real spare money before anyone sold me an investment or a new business as the answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask which money a person is actually willing to risk. A clever tool doesn't get to borrow the family's emergency account. I like a new idea, but I want the children to see that keeping a limit is part of trying it responsibly.

headlineQuote: A clever tool doesn't get to borrow the family's emergency account.
portrait: **Bianca, 43**, is a highly skilled lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence and typical trade pay.
Her **partner works with plants**, with two school-age children, a mortgage, four months saved and some nearby electrical employers.
She uses **AI daily**, welcomes checked experiments and values practical apprenticeships without promising a trade stays safe forever.
Her **small fund plan** uses genuine surplus only, protects the reserve and continuing partner consent, and never substitutes uncertain returns for wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less preparation time before robots around 2031 could reduce both adults' physical-work income.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **paid-hour information** and practical learning while earning would support adjustment.
Clear **costs and genuine surplus** would help her judge financial or business ideas without risking the emergency account.
